title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation
participant_role: Audit senior at a CPA firm auditing KEYSTONE COMPONENTS
judge_role: Chair of the audit committee of KEYSTONE COMPONENTS

difficulty.rationale: Materiality, a scope limitation linked to the right opinion and an independence threat; four tasks fit a 10 minute ICDC role-play.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of audit senior at a CPA firm that is performing the first financial statement audit of KEYSTONE COMPONENTS, a privately held manufacturer of precision metal parts. Keystone's bank requires audited financial statements before it will approve a $5 million loan. The chair of Keystone's audit committee (judge) has asked you for an update on the audit.

Keystone reported pre-tax income of $600,000 for the year. Your firm sets overall materiality at 5% of pre-tax income and performance materiality at 75% of overall materiality.

Your team has made the following findings so far:

(a) Goods shipped on January 2 of the new year were recorded as December sales, overstating pre-tax income by $12,000.
(b) A December utility invoice of $3,000 was never recorded.
(c) Accounts receivable total $1,200,000. The three largest customers owe $480,000 of that amount. The chief financial officer (CFO) refuses to let the auditors send confirmation requests to these three customers, saying "it will annoy them."
(d) A first-year staff accountant assigned to the audit team is the CFO's nephew.

The audit committee chair (judge) has never been through an audit and wants to understand what the audit will and will not tell the bank.

You must:
- Explain what an audit is and the level of assurance it provides
- Calculate materiality and performance materiality and evaluate the misstatements found so far
- Describe the audit procedures your team will use, including for the refused confirmations, and the opinion that will result if the confirmation issue is not resolved
- Address the independence issue on the audit team and explain the audit committee's role in corporate governance

You will present your update to the audit committee chair (judge) in a role-play to take place in Keystone's conference room. The audit committee chair (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your update. After you have presented your update and have answered the chair's (judge's) questions, the audit committee chair (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: If you give us a clean opinion, does that mean there is no fraud?
The CFO says the confirmations are unnecessary because the customers always pay. Why can't you just take his word?

solution.overview: A strong answer defines an audit as reasonable (not absolute) assurance, computes materiality of $30,000 and performance materiality of $22,500, and concludes the $15,000 of misstatements is not material but should still be corrected. It then treats the confirmation refusal as a scope limitation that could lead to a qualified opinion or disclaimer, removes the CFO's nephew from the team, and explains the audit committee's oversight role.

answer: An independent examination of the financial statements and the evidence behind them
Gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance that statements are free of material misstatement under GAAP
Private companies follow AICPA auditing standards (GAAS, issued as SASs); public companies follow PCAOB standards
The bank relies on our opinion to make its $5 million loan decision
Materiality = 5% x 600,000 = $30,000
Performance materiality = 75% x 30,000 = $22,500
Misstatements found: 12,000 + 3,000 = $15,000, below both levels, so not material
Still ask management to correct them and list any uncorrected amounts on the summary of uncorrected misstatements
Cutoff errors suggest we should expand cutoff testing

by_task.task: Audit procedures, the confirmation issue and the resulting opinion
answer: Cutoff testing (shipping documents vs. sales dates around year end) and a search for unrecorded liabilities (January payments and invoices)
Other procedures: inventory observation, analytical procedures, vouching and tracing, inquiry of management and recalculation
Receivables: send confirmations directly to customers; for the three refused customers, try alternative procedures (subsequent cash receipts, invoices and shipping documents)
The CFO's refusal is a scope limitation; $480,000 is 16 times materiality, so report it to the audit committee
Four opinions: unmodified (clean), qualified, adverse, disclaimer
If evidence still cannot be obtained: qualified opinion (material but not pervasive) or disclaimer (pervasive), not a clean opinion

by_task.task: Independence and the audit committee's governance role
answer: Auditors must be independent in fact and in appearance; a family tie to the CFO is a threat to independence
Remove the nephew from the Keystone engagement right away and document the action in the audit file
The audit committee oversees financial reporting and the relationship with the outside auditor
It resolves disagreements between management and the auditors
It makes sure the auditors get full access, including to customers for confirmations
It sets the tone at the top for honest reporting

journal_entries.description: Proposed adjustment: record the unrecorded December utility invoice

judge_question_answers.question: If you give us a clean opinion, does that mean there is no fraud?
answer: No, an audit gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance
Auditors test samples, not every transaction, and collusion or forgery can hide fraud
We look for material misstatement due to fraud, but preventing fraud is management's job through internal controls

judge_question_answers.question: The CFO says the confirmations are unnecessary because the customers always pay. Why can't you just take his word?
answer: Evidence from independent outside parties is more reliable than management's statements
Auditing standards expect receivables to be confirmed unless there is a good reason not to
Professional skepticism requires us to verify, especially with $480,000 at stake
Refusal without a good reason is itself a warning sign we must report to the audit committee

key_concepts.definition: An independent examination of financial statements that ends with an opinion on whether they are fairly presented under GAAP.
A high, but not absolute, level of assurance; auditors test evidence and samples, so they cannot guarantee there are no errors or fraud.
Rules auditors must follow: AICPA standards (Statements on Auditing Standards) for private companies and PCAOB standards for public companies.
The size of a misstatement that could change the decision of a financial statement user. Here, materiality = 5% x pre-tax income.
A lower amount used to plan testing so that small errors together do not become material. Here, 75% x materiality.
Checking that sales and expenses are recorded in the correct period by comparing shipping and receiving documents to dates near year end.
Reviewing payments and invoices after year end to find expenses that belonged in the old year but were not recorded.
A request sent by the auditor directly to a customer asking it to verify the balance it owes.
A restriction that prevents the auditor from gathering enough evidence; it can lead to a qualified opinion or a disclaimer.
Unmodified (clean), qualified (except for one material issue), adverse (statements are materially misstated overall) and disclaimer (no opinion possible).
Being free of relationships that could bias the auditor, both in fact and in appearance, such as a family tie to the CFO.
A board committee that oversees financial reporting, internal control and the outside auditor, and resolves disputes between management and auditors.

notes: ICDC level because the student must apply materiality to real findings, recognize a scope limitation and link it to the right opinion, and handle an independence threat, all while speaking to a nonaccountant. Watch for students who call the $15,000 material, who say the auditor can simply skip the confirmations, or who confuse a qualified opinion (material, not pervasive) with an adverse opinion (misstated) or a disclaimer (pervasive lack of evidence).

items.label: Explain the nature of audits and assurance engagements

criteria.exceeds: Defines an audit as an independent examination of the financial statements and supporting evidence that gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance that they are free of material misstatement under GAAP, and explains that the bank will rely on the opinion for its $5 million loan decision.
criteria.meets: Explains that an audit is an independent examination that provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance about the financial statements.
criteria.below: Describes an audit vaguely, or does not distinguish reasonable from absolute assurance.
criteria.little: Does not explain what an audit is, or says an audit guarantees the statements are completely accurate.

criteria.exceeds: Describes cutoff testing and a search for unrecorded liabilities tied to findings (a) and (b), other procedures such as inventory observation, analytical procedures, vouching and tracing, and alternative procedures for the three refused customers (subsequent cash receipts, invoices and shipping documents), noting the cutoff errors call for expanded cutoff testing.
criteria.meets: Describes confirming receivables directly with customers, alternative procedures for the refused confirmations, and at least cutoff testing and the search for unrecorded liabilities.
criteria.below: Lists procedures generically without linking them to Keystone's findings, or omits alternative procedures for the refused confirmations.
criteria.little: Does not describe audit procedures, or says the auditors can simply skip the confirmations.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates materiality of $30,000 (5% x $600,000) and performance materiality of $22,500, concludes the $15,000 of misstatements is not material but should be corrected (for example debit Utilities Expense $3,000, credit Accounts Payable $3,000), and shows the $480,000 of unconfirmed receivables is 40% of receivables and 16 times materiality.
criteria.meets: Calculates materiality of $30,000 and performance materiality of $22,500 and concludes the $15,000 of misstatements is not material but should still be corrected.
criteria.below: Calculates materiality but calls the $15,000 material, or makes an error in performance materiality.
criteria.little: Does not calculate materiality, or cannot evaluate the misstatements.

items.label: Discuss the nature of auditing/attestation standards

criteria.exceeds: Explains that private companies follow AICPA standards (GAAS, issued as SASs) and public companies follow PCAOB standards, names the four opinions, and explains the refusal is a scope limitation leading to a qualified opinion (material, not pervasive) or a disclaimer (pervasive), not a clean opinion, and that independence in fact and appearance is required.
criteria.meets: Identifies the confirmation refusal as a scope limitation that leads to a qualified opinion or disclaimer if unresolved, and states auditors must be independent.
criteria.below: Knows a clean opinion is not possible but confuses a qualified opinion with an adverse opinion, or cannot name the standards that apply.
criteria.little: Does not discuss standards or opinions, or says a clean opinion can still be issued.

items.label: Discuss the importance of corporate governance in business

criteria.exceeds: Recommends removing the CFO's nephew from the engagement right away and documenting it, and explains that the audit committee oversees financial reporting and the auditor relationship, resolves disagreements, ensures full access for confirmations and sets the tone at the top.
criteria.meets: Removes the nephew from the audit team and explains that the audit committee oversees financial reporting and should make sure the auditors get access to confirm receivables.
criteria.below: Mentions the nephew or the audit committee but gives an incomplete or vague explanation of either.
criteria.little: Ignores the independence issue and the audit committee's role.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects materiality, the scope limitation, the likely opinion and the bank's $5 million loan decision, showing why the CFO's refusal matters far more than the $15,000 of errors.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the findings to the materiality conclusion and the opinion risk.
criteria.below: Reaches conclusions without showing the reasoning, or treats all four findings as equally serious.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives clear next steps: ask the audit committee to secure access for the confirmations, try alternative procedures, correct the $15,000 of errors and remove the nephew, explaining the opinion that results if access is still refused.
criteria.meets: Makes clear recommendations on the confirmations and the nephew.
criteria.below: Gives recommendations that are partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or lets the CFO's refusal and the nephew stand.

criteria.exceeds: Explains materiality, reasonable assurance and the types of opinions in plain language a chair who has never been through an audit can follow, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the update clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on audit jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a simple visual such as a scale comparing the $15,000 of errors and the $480,000 of unconfirmed receivables with the $30,000 materiality line, or a clear chart of the four opinions.
criteria.meets: Organizes the findings in a way that makes their importance easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions confidently: a clean opinion does not mean there is no fraud because an audit gives reasonable assurance, tests samples and can miss collusion or forgery, and preventing fraud is management's job; and the CFO's word is not enough because outside evidence is more reliable, standards expect confirmations, and skepticism is required with $480,000 at stake.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including reasonable versus absolute assurance and why independent evidence is more reliable than management's word.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says a clean opinion proves there is no fraud.

key_points: An audit gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement
Misstatements of $12,000 + $3,000 = $15,000 are not material but should be corrected (debit Utilities Expense $3,000, credit Accounts Payable $3,000)
The $480,000 of unconfirmed receivables is 40% of receivables and 16 times materiality
The CFO's refusal is a scope limitation: try alternative procedures, and if evidence is still lacking issue a qualified opinion or disclaimer, not a clean opinion
Remove the CFO's nephew from the engagement because independence in fact and appearance is required
The audit committee oversees financial reporting and the auditors, resolves disagreements and ensures full access
